implementation_notes: Java's sprawl is the most expensive of any stack here per service, because a Spring Boot application's startup time and heap are large and multiply by the count — the operational maturity the pattern requires (centralised logging, tracing, discovery, orchestration) is not free and is frequently the thing that was skipped. The `microservices` parent module with one submodule per service is the structural form. The consolidation is a modular monolith: one application with several Maven or Gradle modules, which keeps the compile-time boundaries and removes the runtime ones, and which the field guidance treats as delivering faster than a premature microservices architecture for a team that does not need independent deployment.
idiom_name: Spring Boot application per bounded noun; one JVM per service
pitfalls: Three JVMs means three heaps, three GC configurations and three sets of JVM-level security flags to keep current.
Without tracing, a request crossing three services is diagnosed by correlating timestamps across three log streams by hand.
Per-service Flyway migrations into one shared schema is the hidden database coupling that makes consolidation impossible.
